title: Weather, the body, and the pharmacy
title_target: ไม่สบาย — Mâi sà-baai
goal: Talk about the weather, name parts of the body, explain your symptoms to a pharmacist or doctor, and understand the two words that separate "sharp pain" from "throbbing ache".

naming the body parts people most often complain about

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — At the ร้านขายยา in the next soi
dialogs.intro: Budi isn't feeling well after getting caught in the rain. Watch for two words that both mean "pain" but can't be swapped — and how the pharmacist uses them to pin down his symptoms.

notes: **เจ็บ jèp and ปวด pùat both mean "pain", and the difference is real.** *เจ็บ* is pain that's **sharp, from outside, from an injury** — a scratch, a prick, a raw throat: *เจ็บคอ, เจ็บมือ, เจ็บแผล*. *ปวด* is pain that **throbs, from inside**: *ปวดหัว* (headache), *ปวดท้อง* (stomachache), *ปวดฟัน* (toothache), *ปวดหลัง* (backache). ⚠️ Mixing them up can get you the wrong medicine.
**ไม่สบาย mâi sà-baai means "not feeling well"**, an umbrella expression for any illness that isn't serious. Notice that it's the direct opposite of *สบายดี* from unit 1 — the circle closes here.

**เป็นอะไร pen à-rai is "what's wrong?" — not "what's up?".** *เป็น* here carries its second meaning: **to suffer from an illness**, as flagged in unit 2. *เป็นหวัด* (have a cold), *เป็นไข้* (have a fever), *เป็นไข้หวัดใหญ่* (have the flu).

**แพ้ pháae means "allergic" — and also "to lose".** *แพ้ยา* (allergic to medicine), *แพ้อาหารทะเล* (allergic to seafood), *แพ้กุ้ง* (allergic to shrimp). ⚠️ *ผม/ฉันแพ้…ครับ/ค่ะ* is one of the most important sentences for anyone with an allergy to memorize, and you should save it on your phone in Thai script.

**…ขึ้น khûen after an adjective means "getting more…".** *ดีขึ้น* (getting better), *แย่ลง yâae long* (getting worse — with *ลง*, meaning down). The pair *ขึ้น/ลง* is used for many changes: *ร้อนขึ้น* (getting hotter), *ถูกลง* (getting cheaper).
**ครั้ง khráng is the classifier for "times".** *วันละสามครั้ง* (three times a day), *อีกครั้ง* (once more). Dosage instructions almost always use the pattern *วันละ… ครั้ง*.

**หา hǎa means "to look for", but ไปหาหมอ means "go see a doctor"** — literally "go look for the doctor". The pattern *ไปหา + person* is the standard way to say "visit someone": *ไปหาเพื่อน* (go see a friend).

**The ร้านขายยา ráan khǎai yaa (pharmacy) is the first place Thai people go**, not the hospital. Thai pharmacists are used to hearing symptoms and putting together a *ยาชุด yaa chút* — a small bag of medicine for a few days. For minor complaints, this is much faster and cheaper.

grammars.title: The body parts people most often complain about
after: ⚠️ **หัว *hǔa* (head) and หู *hǔu* (ear) differ only in the vowel**, and both have a rising tone. Practice them side by side: *hǔa — hǔu*.

Remember the cultural rule from unit 12: **the head is the highest part of the body and must not be touched**, not even a child's; **the feet are the lowest** and must not be pointed at people or at Buddha images.

after: **Emergency phrases to memorize word for word:** *ช่วยด้วย chûai dûai* (help!), *เรียกรถพยาบาลหน่อย rîak rót-phá-yaa-baan nàwy* (call an ambulance), *ผม/ฉันแพ้… phǒm/chǎn pháae …* (I'm allergic to …).
Emergency numbers in Thailand: **191** for police, **1669** for an ambulance, **1155** for the English-speaking tourist police.

grammars.title: Weather and the three seasons
after: **หน้า nâa here means "season"** — the third meaning of a word that also means "front" and "face". Thai really does like to give one word many jobs.

⚠️ **Thailand's "cold season" isn't cold by European standards** — in Bangkok it means about 22–25 degrees. But up north, Chiang Mai and its mountains really can drop to 10 degrees, and locals wear thick jackets. For anyone from the tropics, that genuinely feels cold.

blocks.text: The weather is the safest small-talk topic anywhere, and Thailand is no different. These four sentences work with anyone.

items: **วันนี้ร้อนจังนะครับ/คะ** — it's so hot today, isn't it?
**ฝนจะตกแล้ว** *fǒn jà tòk láaeo* — it's about to rain.
**เอาร่มไปด้วยนะครับ/คะ** — take an umbrella, okay?
**อากาศดีนะครับ/คะ** — nice weather, isn't it?

blocks.title: The rainy season isn't rain all day
items: In the rainy season, Bangkok's rain usually comes down hard for an hour or two in the late afternoon, then stops. It's not the all-day rain newcomers imagine.

What to watch out for is **น้ำท่วม *náam thûam*** — flooding — which can make roads impassable for a few hours. Useful phrases: *น้ำท่วมไหมครับ/คะ* (is it flooded?) and *รถผ่านได้ไหมครับ/คะ rót phàan dâai mǎi* (can cars get through?).
A folding umbrella in the bag is a habit almost every Thai person keeps — and it's used for both rain and sun.

blocks.title: Three practical points
items: **Bring your passport.** Thai hospitals register patients under their passport name, and without it the process stops at the first desk.
**Private hospitals are much faster and English-speaking**, but they can cost several times more. Public hospitals (*โรงพยาบาลรัฐ*) are far cheaper, with long lines.
**Keep your allergies written in Thai script on your phone.** For example: *ฉันแพ้ยาเพนนิซิลลิน* (I'm allergic to penicillin). In an emergency, showing a screen is much faster than speaking.
